title: Production Deployment
readme:
FULL STACK DEVELOPER 2026 - Phase 34
Production Deployment

Primary deployment topology:
  Web  -> Vercel
  API  -> Railway (immutable GHCR image)
  Data/Auth/Storage/Realtime -> Supabase production project

The phase includes focused books, one combined book, environment templates, production runbooks, platform notes, and smoke-test assets.

lessons.body:
Production Topology, Environments, and Release
Identity
Use distinct local, staging, and production environments so a preview does not accidentally point at production data.
Keep the deployment identity visible everywhere: commit SHA, API image tag, Vercel deployment, migration batch,
and monitoring release.

local
→         staging
→         production

Figure 2 - Environment promotion, not environment sharing

Recommended production addresses
• https://app.taskflow.example.com -> Next.js on Vercel

• https://api.taskflow.example.com -> NestJS on Railway

• Supabase production project -> PostgreSQL, Auth, Storage, Realtime

Release identity
• API image: ghcr.io/<org>/<repo>-api:sha-<commit>

• Web deployment: verified main commit on Vercel

• Sentry/release metadata: same Git commit SHA

• Database migration: committed Prisma migration set from the same release
A preview environment should use staging credentials and staging data. Do not solve preview convenience by giving
every preview URL production secrets.

Source basis: platform environment/deployment models plus TaskFlow release architecture from Phases 32-33.

Core configuration
• Root Directory: apps/web

• Production branch: main

• Production domain: app.taskflow.example.com

• Preview deployments may point to staging services, not the production API/database

Public vs server-only configuration
• NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and the publishable key are browser configuration.

• NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL is safe only because it is a public endpoint address, not a credential.

• Never expose service-role keys or database credentials through NEXT_PUBLIC_*.
NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL=https://app.taskflow.example.com
NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=https://api.taskflow.example.com
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=https://<project-ref>.supabase.co

SENTRY_DSN=<server-side-if-used>

NEXT_PUBLIC_* values are embedded into browser output at build time. Changing them normally requires a new web
deployment.

lessons.summary: Railway: Deploy the NestJS API from GHCR The API follows the build-once path from Phase 33: Railway pulls the exact GHCR image tagged with the Git SHA. When Railway uses a Docker-image source, it skips its own source build so the artifact tested in CI…
lessons.body:
Railway: Deploy the NestJS API from GHCR
The API follows the build-once path from Phase 33: Railway pulls the exact GHCR image tagged with the Git SHA.
When Railway uses a Docker-image source, it skips its own source build so the artifact tested in CI is the artifact that
runs.

GHCR sha image
→      Railway service
→       /health/ready
→   Traffic switch

Figure 4 - Immutable API promotion

Service rules
• Source: exact GHCR image tag, not :latest

• Listen on 0.0.0.0 and process.env.PORT

• Healthcheck path: /health/ready

• Custom domain: api.taskflow.example.com with automatic TLS

Registry credentials
• Private GHCR images require Railway private-registry support and a read-only package token.

• Do not reuse the CI token that has write:packages.

• A public image avoids registry credentials but may not suit a proprietary application.
# Container runtime concept
HOST=0.0.0.0
PORT=<injected by Railway>
NODE_ENV=production

# Image identity
ghcr.io/acme/taskflow-api:sha-<full-commit>

Railway health checks gate the new deployment before traffic is switched, but Railway documents that this
healthcheck is deployment-time gating rather than continuous post-deploy monitoring.

Sources: Railway private registry deployment, service-source, domain, healthcheck, and rollback documentation.

lessons.body:
Supabase Production Project and Database
Configuration
Create a production Supabase project separate from local/staging. Production schema changes come from
version-controlled migrations; the dashboard is not the authoritative migration tool after launch.

Committed
Migration job               Production DB              API release
migration
→                           →                              →
Figure 5 - Database changes are part of the release

Production checklist
• Review Security Advisor and Performance Advisor findings.

• Use indexes that match measured query patterns and monitor connection usage.

• Plan backups/PITR according to business requirements and database size.

• Restrict who can change production and prefer migrations through CI/deployment workflows.

Connection strategy
• Application runtime uses the connection/pool mode appropriate to the always-on NestJS topology.

• Migration tooling should use a connection mode that supports migration operations reliably.

• Do not create one PrismaClient per request; retain the singleton service architecture from earlier phases.
Supabase runs the managed platform; TaskFlow still owns query design, indexes, connection behavior, application
authorization, and safe production-change practices.

lessons.body:
Environment Variables, Secrets, Domains, TLS,
and CORS
Configuration is environment-specific; secrets are never browser configuration. Both Vercel and Railway can
provision HTTPS for custom domains, but CORS still has to match the API trust model.

Variable                             Location                         Purpose

NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL                 Vercel public                    Canonical web origin

NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL                  Vercel public                    Public API base URL

DATABASE_URL                         Railway secret                   Production PostgreSQL connection

SUPABASE_URL                         Railway config                   Production Supabase project URL

SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY            Railway secret                   Server-only Storage/admin operations

CORS_ORIGIN                          Railway config                   Exact production web origin

SENTRY_DSN                           Both as needed                   Production error reporting

Domain plan
• app.taskflow.example.com -> Vercel

• api.taskflow.example.com -> Railway

• TLS is platform-managed after DNS verification

• Production API CORS should prefer the exact production origin, not * with credentials

Preview warning
• Do not whitelist arbitrary *.vercel.app origins against production just to make previews convenient.

• Use staging API/Supabase for previews, or explicitly enumerate controlled preview access if a product requirement truly
needs it.
A URL is public configuration. A credential is secret. Keeping that distinction clear prevents many deployment leaks.

Sources: Vercel environment scopes; Railway custom domains/automatic SSL; TaskFlow Phase 29 security model.

Supabase Auth: Redirect URLs, Site URL,
Cookies, and Sessions
Authentication often breaks only after deployment because localhost redirect assumptions remain in the Auth project.
Production Auth configuration must know the canonical web URL and every intentional callback.

Sign in
→      Supabase Auth
→      Allowed redirect
→        /auth/confirm
→   Session cookie

Figure 6 - Production authentication redirect chain

Production URL configuration
• Site URL: https://app.taskflow.example.com

• Add exact production redirect paths used by confirmation/OAuth/reset flows.

• Use preview wildcards only for preview environments and keep production redirects exact where possible.

• Verify email templates use the intended redirect value when redirectTo is used.

Session checks
• Cookies must be Secure over HTTPS.

• Cross-site/cross-origin behavior must match the Phase 16-18 authentication model.

• A successful web login does not replace NestJS bearer-token verification; the API still validates identity independently.
A correct production domain is part of authentication correctness. Redirect allowlists are security configuration, not
cosmetic routing.

lessons.title: Migration Order Backward Compatibility and Release Sequence
lessons.summary: Migration Order, Backward Compatibility, and Release Sequence Database deployment is where rollback gets difficult. Prefer expand-migrate-contract changes so the old application and the new application can coexist during rollout and rollback windows. Expand schema → Migrate data → Deploy code → Observe → Contract later…
lessons.body:
Migration Order, Backward Compatibility, and
Release Sequence
Database deployment is where rollback gets difficult. Prefer expand-migrate-contract changes so the old application
and the new application can coexist during rollout and rollback windows.

Expand schema
→       Migrate data
→        Deploy code
→           Observe
→       Contract later

Figure 7 - Safer database evolution

Release ordering
• 1. Validate production configuration and backups/recovery posture.

• 2. Run prisma migrate deploy as a one-off migration job.

• 3. Deploy the API SHA image and wait for readiness.

• 4. Deploy/promote the web application.

• 5. Run smoke tests and watch telemetry.

Avoid fragile migrations
• Do not rename/drop a column in the same instant the old API might still use it.

• Add new structures first, deploy compatible code, migrate data, then remove obsolete structures in a later release.

• A code rollback cannot magically reverse destructive database changes.
# Migration release step
pnpm --filter api exec prisma migrate deploy

# Only after success:
# - promote API image
# - promote web deployment

Rollback-friendly deployment starts with rollback-friendly schema changes.

Source basis: Prisma deployment workflow from earlier phases plus production-safe expand/migrate/contract release practice.

lessons.summary: Health, Readiness, Zero-Downtime Promotion, and Graceful Shutdown A process can be alive but not ready. Deployment platforms should route traffic only after the new version is ready, and the old version should have time to finish work during termination. Start new version → /health/ready 2xx…
lessons.body:
Health, Readiness, Zero-Downtime Promotion, and
Graceful Shutdown
A process can be alive but not ready. Deployment platforms should route traffic only after the new version is ready,
and the old version should have time to finish work during termination.

Start new version
→     /health/ready 2xx
→        Switch traffic
→        SIGTERM old
→       Graceful exit

Figure 8 - Health-gated promotion

Endpoints
• /health/live: process is alive; avoid making it fail because PostgreSQL is briefly unavailable.

• /health/ready: operation-critical dependencies such as PostgreSQL are available.

• Never require user authentication for platform health probes.

Platform behavior
• Railway waits for a successful 2xx healthcheck before making the new deployment active.

• Render can also use HTTP health checks to decide whether a new web-service deployment is ready for traffic.

• Phase 30 observability still monitors health after rollout; deployment probes are not a substitute for alerts.
Readiness gates traffic. Liveness decides whether the process itself should be considered alive. Mixing them creates
unnecessary restarts during dependency incidents.

Storage and Realtime Production Configuration
The production Supabase project must carry the same security architecture already established for Storage and
Realtime. Deployment is where local convenience policies must be removed.

Storage
• Create the private task-attachments bucket with production MIME/size restrictions.

• Keep service-role access server-only.

• Signed download URLs stay short-lived.

• Run orphan-cleanup/reconciliation jobs with explicit observability.

Realtime
• Deploy Broadcast triggers and Realtime authorization policies through version-controlled database changes.

• Use private workspace topics and production user membership checks.

• After reconnect, invalidate/refetch authoritative HTTP data as taught in Phase 26.

Production validation
• Test a member and non-member against Realtime topics.

• Test attachment upload/finalize/download/delete against real production-like configuration before public launch.

• Confirm no public bucket or permissive channel policy was accidentally carried from development.
Supabase services are infrastructure capabilities. NestJS/PostgreSQL remain the application source of truth and
authorization authority.

lessons.body:
Rollback, Recovery, and Incident Decisions
A rollback plan must exist before the release. Roll back application code quickly when code/config is the cause; treat
database/schema incidents separately because destructive migrations may not be reversible by restoring an old
image.

Investigate root
Bad release             Stop promotion              Rollback app              Verify health
→                         →                          →                       →           cause

Figure 10 - Recovery path

API rollback
• Railway can roll back to a previous successful deployment while restoring that deployment's image and custom variables
within the platform retention window.

• Use the last known-good immutable SHA, then rerun smoke checks.

Web rollback
• Promote a known-good previous Vercel deployment or redeploy the known-good commit according to team policy.

• Keep production environment variables version/change-controlled operationally even though they live outside Git.

Database incident
• Do not assume an application rollback fixes a destructive migration.

• Use backup/PITR or a forward-fix migration according to the incident runbook.

• This is why expand-contract and tested migrations are part of deployment design.
Rollback is a capability, not a strategy. Recovery decisions depend on whether the failure is code, configuration, data,
migration, dependency, or infrastructure.

Goal

lessons.body:
Debugging Workshop — Phase 34: Production Deployment

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk

lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Production Deployment

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 34 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Deploy the real topology—Next.js, NestJS image, Supabase services, migrations, domains/TLS/CORS, secrets, health checks, smoke tests, and rollback—as one release system.

Required artifact
Staging and production deployment runbooks with release identity, environment matrix, smoke tests, and rollback procedure.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can describe the whole topology.
• Can separate environment configuration.
• Can execute smoke tests.
• Can explain code vs database rollback constraints.

Independent build sequence
1. Create separate staging/production environment matrices before entering any dashboard values.
2. Deploy Next.js from the intended monorepo root with public/server env vars separated.
3. Deploy the exact API container artifact and verify bind address, PORT, and readiness endpoint.
4. Apply database migrations as a controlled release step and document backward-compatibility assumptions.
5. Configure custom domains/TLS and the exact CORS/redirect origins for production.
6. Run a smoke-test checklist and practice rollback of code while reasoning about whether the database migration is reversible.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 34: Production Deployment. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact
Staging and production deployment runbooks with release identity, environment matrix, smoke tests, and rollback procedure.

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

# TaskFlow Production Deployment Runbook

## Preflight
1. Required CI checks are green for the exact release commit.
2. Verify production environment variables and secret scopes.
3. Verify Supabase production Site URL and redirect allowlist.
4. Confirm recovery posture: recent backup/PITR where required.
5. Review Prisma migrations for backward compatibility.

## Deploy
1. Run `prisma migrate deploy` as a one-off production migration job.
2. Promote the exact API image `sha-<commit>` to Railway.
3. Wait for `/health/ready` to pass.
4. Promote/deploy the matching verified web commit on Vercel.
5. Run smoke tests.
6. Observe 5xx, p95 latency, readiness, database signals, and Sentry.

## Rollback
- If API code/config is broken, roll Railway back to the last known-good deployment/image and rerun smoke tests.
- If web code/config is broken, promote a known-good previous Vercel deployment/commit.

# Production Environment Matrix

| Variable | Web | API | Secret? | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL | yes | no | no | Canonical web origin |
| NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL | yes | no | no | Public API origin |
| NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL | yes | no | no | Public project URL |
| NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY | yes | no | no | Browser-safe public key |
| DATABASE_URL | no | yes | yes | Production Postgres connection |
| SUPABASE_URL | no | yes | no | Production project URL |
| SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY | no | yes | yes | Server only |
| CORS_ORIGIN | no | yes | no | Exact production web origin |
| SENTRY_DSN | as needed | as needed | treat carefully | Production telemetry |

Never use `NEXT_PUBLIC_` for database credentials, service-role keys, registry tokens, or other secrets.

# TaskFlow Production Topology

- Web: `https://app.taskflow.example.com` -> Vercel (`apps/web`)
- API: `https://api.taskflow.example.com` -> Railway Docker image service
- Data/Auth/Storage/Realtime: separate production Supabase project

## Environment rule

Local, staging, and production use separate configuration. Preview deployments must not receive production credentials merely for convenience.

## Release identity

Use the same Git commit SHA in API image tags, release notes, error monitoring, and deployment records.

# TaskFlow Production Deployment Snapshot

This snapshot is a study/reference package for Phase 34. Replace `taskflow.example.com`, project references, image paths, and secrets with real environment values.

Primary course topology:
- Next.js -> Vercel
- NestJS/Fastify -> Railway from GHCR SHA image
- PostgreSQL/Auth/Storage/Realtime -> Supabase production project

Render is documented as an API-host alternative.

# Source Notes

Current source basis verified during Phase 34 generation:

- Vercel environment configuration and deployment protection guidance.
- Railway Docker-image sources, GHCR private registries, deployment health checks, domains, rollback behavior.
- Render Docker web-service and HTTP health-check documentation as the API-host alternative.
- Supabase production checklist, shared responsibility model, maturity model, Auth redirect URLs, and security configuration guidance.

The course topology and release decisions remain TaskFlow architecture choices; provider behavior should be rechecked before a future production launch because cloud platforms evolve.

# Supabase Production Checklist for TaskFlow

- Use a production project separate from local/staging.
- Set Auth Site URL to the canonical production web origin.
- Add exact production Auth redirect paths.
- Review Security Advisor and Performance Advisor.
- Apply schema through version-controlled migrations.
- Verify indexes and connection topology under expected load.
- Configure private Storage bucket rules used by Task attachments.
- Deploy Realtime Broadcast triggers and authorization policies.
- Review backups/PITR and access controls appropriate to the business.

NODE_ENV=production
# PORT is injected by Railway. The app must listen on 0.0.0.0:$PORT.
DATABASE_URL=replace-with-production-connection
SUPABASE_URL=https://PROJECT_REF.supabase.co
SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=replace-with-public-key
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY=replace-with-server-only-secret
CORS_ORIGIN=https://app.taskflow.example.com
# SENTRY_DSN=...

# Railway API Service

- Source: Docker Image
- Image: `ghcr.io/<org>/<repo>-api:sha-<full-commit>`
- Healthcheck: `/health/ready`
- Public domain: `api.taskflow.example.com`
- Keep GHCR pull credentials read-only.
- Do not use `:latest` for production application releases.
- Railway health checks gate new deployments before traffic promotion.

# Render Alternative for the API

Render can host the NestJS Docker web service as an alternative to Railway. Configure the service to listen on `0.0.0.0` and the platform port, set an HTTP health-check path such as `/health/ready`, and attach the custom API domain. Render uses health checks when deciding whether a new web-service deployment can receive traffic.

Keep the same application-level architecture and production environment separation regardless of platform.

param(
  [string]$Web = "https://app.taskflow.example.com",
  [string]$Api = "https://api.taskflow.example.com"
)

$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"

Write-Host "Checking API liveness..."
Invoke-WebRequest "$Api/health/live" -UseBasicParsing | Out-Null

Write-Host "Checking API readiness..."
Invoke-WebRequest "$Api/health/ready" -UseBasicParsing | Out-Null

Write-Host "Checking web sign-in route..."
Invoke-WebRequest "$Web/sign-in" -UseBasicParsing | Out-Null

Write-Host "PASS: unauthenticated production smoke checks"
Write-Host "Run the authenticated smoke flow separately with a controlled test identity."

# Production Verification Matrix

| Check | Expected |
|---|---|
| Web custom domain | HTTPS + expected production app |
| API `/health/live` | 2xx |
| API `/health/ready` | 2xx when DB is available |
| Auth sign in | Session established |
| Auth confirmation/reset | Returns to production domain |
| GET /tasks as member | Only authorized rows |
| Cross-workspace ID | 403/404 according to policy |
| Create/update test Task | Persists after reload |
| Attachment flow | Private upload/download works |
| Realtime flow | Authorized peer receives refresh signal |
| 5xx / Sentry | No unexpected release regression |
| Rollback rehearsal | Known-good version restored |
